title: Clean hands (Psalm 24)
hookLine: who may climb the mountain? "He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart"

cards: Some doors you can't just walk through. A surgeon scrubs before the operating room. A guest knocks before entering a friend's home.
A candidate prepares for an interview. Some places ask something of you before you go in. Now go back to Jerusalem, to pilgrims at the foot of the Temple hill, looking up.
In one reading of Psalm twenty-four, someone calls out a question, and the crowd answers.

teach.b: The psalm opens by saying the whole earth belongs to God, and everyone in it. Then the question: "Who shall ascend into the mountain of the LORD?" Who shall stand in His holy place?
The answer: "He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart". In Hebrew: neki khapayim u-var levav. Notice what isn't on the list: the richest, the most learned, the right family.
The entrance requirements are hands and heart.
Hands are what you do: how you treat people, what you take, what you give, whether your business is honest. The psalm spells it out: someone who hasn't sworn deceitfully.
The heart is what's going on inside: your intentions, whether you mean it. Both matter. Clean hands with a hidden agenda aren't enough.
A good heart that never acts isn't either.

teach.h: LIFT UP YOUR HEADS, O GATES.
teach.b: Then the psalm bursts into drama: lift up your heads, O ye gates, that the King of glory may come in. Who is the King of glory?
Some scholars think this was sung antiphonally, one group calling, another answering, maybe as the ark came up to Jerusalem.
Today, in a common synagogue custom, it's sung as the Torah scroll is carried back to the ark on weekdays: the gates lift, and the Torah goes home.
And Jewish life has a daily echo of clean hands: the ritual washing on waking and before eating bread, with a blessing. The washing isn't about dirt. It's about what the hands do next.

how: In a common synagogue custom, Psalm 24 is sung as the Torah is returned to the ark on weekdays, and observant Jews wash their hands ritually, with a blessing, on waking and before eating bread.

o: honest actions, the first thing asked at God's gate
being born into the right priestly family
giving charity before entering the Temple

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.

s: 'clean hands' in Psalm 24 is about hygiene
it's about actions: honesty, not swearing deceitfully.
the psalm's entry requirements include wealth and good family
only hands and heart are on the list.
Psalm 24 is sung in synagogue as the Torah returns to the ark on weekdays
it's a common custom: lift up your heads, O ye gates, as the Torah goes home.

games.q: you're at the foot of the mountain of the Lord. a voice calls: who may climb? what's the answer?
o: clean hands and a pure heart.
games.why: Psalm 24: he that hath clean hands, and a pure heart. what you do, and what you mean.

practice: At a sink now, or the next time you wash, let the water run slowly over your hands and think of one thing they'll do today, write, cook, hold someone, fix something, type a message, and ask that it be clean: honest, kind.
Then dry them and notice your heart: what do you mean by the day ahead? If you pray, you can say so to God.

wordCard.voice: Clean hands. Psalm twenty-four's answer to who may climb the mountain of the Lord: clean hands, and a pure heart. What you do, and what you mean.

orig.note: Hebrew: clean of hands and pure of heart, from Psalm 24:4.

carryVoice: Your line: clean hands, pure heart. Hands and heart, together at the gate. Until tomorrow, then.
